questions.question: What is the path difference between two consecutive half-period zones?
questions.solution_html:
• MG4DSCPHY200 - W ave Optics Scheme for Valuation - MGU March 2026
  • Air (n0 = 1)
  • Surface 1
  • Surface 2
  • Film (n)
  • Air (n0 = 1)
  • Incident
  • Ray 1 (π shift)
  • 2nt cos θr
  • Ray 2 (no shift)
  • Figure 3: Thin-film interference. Ray 1 reflects from the top surface with a π phase shift; Ray 2 traverses
  • the film twice with optical path 2nt cos θr and no phase shift at the bottom surface. Their superposition
  • produces constructive or destructive interference.
  • Setup. A thin transparent film of thickness t and refractive index n (n > nair = 1) is surrounded by
  • air on both sides. Light of wavelength λ (in vacuum) is incident at angle θi in air. By Snell’s law, the
  • refraction angle inside the film is θr where sin θi = n sin θr.
  • Two Reflected Rays.
  • • Ray 1 reflects from the top surface(air → film, going from lower n to higher n): undergoes a phase
  • shift of π (half-wave loss), equivalent to an extra optical path of λ/2.
  • • Ray 2 refracts into the film, reflects from the bottom surface (film → air, going from higher n to
  • lower n): no phase shift on reflection. Ray 2 then refracts back out through the top surface.
  • Optical Path Difference. The path traversed by Ray 2 inside the film (going down and back up) is
  • 2t/ cos θr (geometric path in the film), but must be multiplied by the film’s refractive index n to get
  • the optical path. Correcting also for the lateral shift, the net optical path difference between Rays 1
  • and 2 is ( Hecht, §9.4):
  • ∆optical = 2nt cos θr
  • Including the π phase shift of Ray 1 (equivalent to + λ/2), the effective path difference is:
  • ∆eff = 2nt cos θr + λ2
  • Conditions for Constructive Interference (Bright reflection): Constructive interference requires
  • the effective path difference to equal an integer number of wavelengths:
  • 2nt cos θr + λ2 = mλ, m = 1, 2, 3, . . .
  • ∴ 2nt cos θr =
  • m − 12  λ = (2m − 1)λ2
  • Conditions for Destructive Interference (Dark / no reflection): Destructive interference re-
  • quires the effective path difference to equal a half-integer multiple of λ:
  • 2nt cos θr + λ2 = m + 12  λ
  • ∴ 2nt cos θr = mλ , m = 0, 1, 2, . . .

questions.question: Discuss the dependence of the width of the central diffraction maximum on the wavelength of light in single-slit diffraction.
questions.solution_html:
• MG4DSCPHY200 - W ave Optics Scheme for Valuation - MGU March 2026
  • When the wavelength is large compared to the aperture, the wavelets interfere constructively over
  • a wide angular range, causing the wave to spread broadly into the shadow region. This explains the
  • strong diffraction of sound around everyday objects.
  • When the wavelength is small compared to the aperture, constructive interference is confined to a
  • narrow forward cone, and a well-defined geometric shadow is formed. This explains why light appears
  • to travel in straight lines under ordinary conditions.

  • Q21

  • hofer double-slit diffraction. O4]
  • Young’s double-slit experiment treats the slits as infinitesimally narrow (ideal) point sources and con-
  • siders only the interference between the two beams. Fraunhofer double-slit diffraction is the more
  • physically accurate treatment that accounts for the finite width b of each slit, leading to a pattern that
  • is the product of a single-slit diffraction envelope and a two-slit interference pattern ( Hecht, §9.3.1
  • and §10.2.2).
  • A. Young’s Double-Slit — Intensity Formula.
  • The two infinitely narrow slits separated by a act as coherent line sources. The irradiance at angle θ is:

  • B. Fraunhofer Double-Slit — Intensity Formula.
  • Each slit of width b produces its own single-slit diffraction pattern. The combined intensity is the
  • product of the single-slit diffraction envelope and the two-slit interference pattern:
  • I(θ) = 4I0

questions.question: Explain polarisation by scattering.
questions.solution_html:
• Q22
  • Describe the construction of a zone plate. O4]
  • A zone plate is an optical device that focuses light by the principle of diffraction, unlike a conventional
  • lens which focuses light by refraction. It is constructed based on the concept of Fresnel half-period zones
  • and works by blocking out alternate zones so that only constructive interference contributions reach the
  • focal point, resulting in a bright focused spot ( Hecht, §10.3.5).
  • Concept of Fresnel Half-Period Zones Consider a plane wavefront advancing toward a point of
  • observation P . The wavefront can be divided into a series of concentric circular zones called Fresnel
  • half-period zones, such that the distance from the outer edge of each successive zone to P differs by λ/2
  • from the previous one. If r1, r2, r3, are the radii of successive zones, then the path difference between
  • consecutive zones is λ/2. The contributions from alternate zones are in opposite phase, meaning odd
  • zones and even zones tend to cancel each other out. The resultant amplitude at P due to the entire
  • unobstructed wavefront is therefore only about half the contribution of the first zone alone.
  • Radius of the nth Fresnel zone:
  • Rm =
  • mr0λ
  • where:
  • m is zone number, λ wavelength of light, r0 distance from the wavefront to the point of observation P
  • A zone plate is constructed by first drawing a highly magnified diagram on paper with concentric
  • circles having radii proportional to
  • 2, · · ·representing the boundaries of successive Fresnel
  • half-period zones. Alternate zones are then shaded black while the remaining zones are left transparent,
  • producing a pattern of alternating opaque and transparent concentric rings. This drawing is then
  • photographed and reduced to a very small size using photographic techniques, ensuring that the zone
  • radii are of the order of millimetres or less, appropriate for use with visible light. The developed
  • photographic film or glass plate with this pattern of alternating opaque and transparent rings constitutes
  • the finished zone plate, which can then be mounted and used in place of a converging lens.
  • Focal Length The zone plate acts as a converging lens with focal length: f1 = R2m
  • mλ It produces multiple
  • focal points at f, f /3, f /5, · · ·unlike a simple lens which has only one focal point.
  • A zone plate is constructed by blocking alternate Fresnel zones on a photographic plate. It focuses
  • light by diffraction and serves as a diffractive equivalent of a converging lens, with the unique property
  • of possessing multiple focal points.
